prompt: A word occurs much more often in spam than in legitimate email. What additional information is needed to interpret an email containing that word?

options.text: Only the number of letters in the word.
options.explanation: Length is not the supplied class-evidence model.

options.text: The class prior, together with the word’s rate in both classes.
options.explanation: Posterior class probability depends on base rates and comparative evidence.
That likelihood alone does not compare competing explanations.

options.text: Only whether the word appears twice.
options.explanation: Repetition still needs a feature model and class probabilities.

workedExample: The word favours spam because it is more characteristic of spam, but the prior determines how much spam existed to begin with. Also specify whether the rates describe document presence or token frequency; they cannot be swapped.

prompt: Two words commonly occur together as a fixed phrase even within spam messages. A naive Bayes model treats their presence as independent within each class. What is the main risk?

options.text: It may count overlapping evidence twice and give overly extreme probabilities.
options.explanation: Within-class feature dependence violates the naive assumption.

options.text: It must fail to rank every email correctly.
options.explanation: Approximate independence can still yield useful classifications.
Class priors still contribute to scores.

options.text: Adding any second feature is forbidden.
options.explanation: Multiple features are the point; their dependence needs attention.

workedExample: Ask whether the second word is surprising after the first word and class are known. If the phrase makes it predictable, multiplying unchanged individual likelihoods exaggerates the amount of distinct evidence. Evaluate calibration separately from ranking quality.
